factCheck.evidence: Van Cleave's open textbook says logic and critical thinking centrally involve the analysis and assessment of arguments; the SEP's Logical Consequence entry describes logic's study of the 'follows from' relation between premises and conclusions.
Merriam-Webster's etymology: from Latin logica, from Greek logike, from logikos 'of reason', from logos 'reason'.

Dewey's How We Think (Project Gutenberg text) gives the definition verbatim; the University of Hong Kong's critical thinking course also traces critical thinking in education to Dewey's 'reflective thinking' with the same wording.
The SEP's Critical Thinking entry quotes the same definition (Dewey 1910: 6) and says the term's use as an educational goal goes back to Dewey; the HKU course page quotes it too.
The University of Hong Kong's page on definitions of critical thinking quotes the same sentence from Dewey (1910), How We Think, p. 74.

Van Cleave's textbook contrasts an argument as a heated exchange of views with logic's sense, a reason for thinking a statement is true; the IEP notes 'argument' can mean a dispute or be used technically.
forall x says belligerent shouting matches are not arguments in logic's sense, just disagreements; Van Cleave draws the same contrast.
The IEP characterizes an argument as a collection of truth-bearers some of which are offered as reasons for one of them, the conclusion; the APA blog gives the same textbook definition.
Van Cleave's textbook gives the same definition: premises attempt to provide a reason for thinking the conclusion is true.
The IEP: a collection of propositions lacks the structure of an argument unless a reasoner puts forward some as reasons in support of another.
The APA blog: an argument is distinct from abuse and from mere contradiction; the IEP: propositions form an argument only if some are offered as reasons for another.
Wikipedia: the sketch first aired in 'The Money Programme' on 2 November 1972, and the exchange consists mostly of contradictory 'is/isn't' responses; the MIT handout's transcript shows the same.

The MIT philosophy handout quotes the line 'An argument is a connected series of statements intended to establish a proposition' and uses it to define argument; Wikipedia notes the line was taken almost verbatim from the Oxford English Dictionary.
forall x defines a sentence, for logic, as one that can be true or false; the IEP calls premises and conclusions truth-bearers.
Van Cleave: a statement is a type of sentence that can be true or false; a false sentence is still a statement.

forall x: logic is only interested in sentences that can figure as premise or conclusion, i.e. sentences that can be true or false; the IEP says an imperative is not truth-apt and so is not a component of an argument.
Van Cleave: questions such as 'Do you like Vietnamese pho?' are not statements because it doesn't make sense to ask whether they are true or false.
Van Cleave: requests and commands such as 'Don't tell your mother about the surprise' are not statements; the IEP: the imperative 'Let's look there!' is not truth-apt.
College of San Mateo's critical thinking tutorial: statements of fact put forward verifiable assertions; to evaluate one, you verify the information.
Wikipedia's fact-value distinction: statements of fact (descriptive statements) are based on reason and observation.
College of San Mateo's tutorial lists statements such as 'Peanut butter is made from boiled walrus' and says some are true and some are not, but all are statements of fact.
College of San Mateo's tutorial contrasts objective facts with subjective matters such as whether something tastes good, where there is no real right or wrong.
Wikipedia's fact-value distinction: statements of value (normative or prescriptive statements), such as good and bad, contrast with statements of fact (descriptive statements).
Van Cleave: the reason for thinking the conclusion is true is called the premise; forall x names premises and conclusion the same way.
The IEP: the reasons offered within the argument are called premises, and the proposition they are offered for is called the conclusion.
Merriam-Webster: premise from Medieval Latin praemissa, from Latin praemittere 'to place ahead', from prae- + mittere 'to send'.
Merriam-Webster: conclude from Latin concludere 'to shut up, end, infer', from com- + claudere 'to shut'.
The IEP: in standard form the premises are listed first and a line separates them from the conclusion, prefaced by the 'therefore' symbol; the APA blog describes regimenting an argument the same way.
Van Cleave: standard argument form numbers the premises and ends with the conclusion, denoted by 'therefore'; forall x reads the three dots as 'therefore'.

Van Cleave's example puts the conclusion first ('Abortion is morally wrong because...', conclusion = the first four words) and his single-sentence arguments ('Tom was sleeping, so he couldn't have answered the phone') show one sentence can hold an argument.
Van Cleave's table lists therefore, so, hence, thus and consequently as conclusion indicators; the IEP lists therefore, thus, hence and so.
forall x and Van Cleave give the same conclusion indicators (so, therefore, hence, thus, consequently).
Van Cleave's table lists since, because, for, as and given that as premise indicators; the IEP lists because, since, for and as.
forall x lists since, because and given that; Van Cleave adds for and as.
The IEP: these expressions do not always function as indicators, so their mere use does not necessitate the presence of an argument.
Van Cleave: indicators are not failsafe; 'since 1999' and 'so happy' contain them without any argument.
Merriam-Webster defines enthymeme as a syllogism in which one of the premises is implicit.
The APA blog describes students supplying 'implicit premises' when regimenting the Argument Clinic argument; the IEP describes suppressed premises in enthymemes.
The APA blog says implicit premises are demanded by the principle of charity; the IEP says charity dictates how an invalid argument should be read.
The SEP on Hume: on the dominant reading, no ought-judgment may be correctly inferred from premises expressed only in terms of 'is', so a 'should' conclusion needs an evaluative premise.
The IEP: in presenting an explanation the reasoner believes the thing explained is already accepted by the audience, while an argument presents a standpoint not yet accepted.
Van Cleave: in an explanation we assume that what we are trying to explain is true, and explanations give us an understanding of why it is true.
Van Cleave's obesity example makes the same point: premises that give a reason why an accepted claim is true form an explanation, not an argument that it is true.
Van Cleave: very often arguments have a more complex structure, in which a statement that supports the main conclusion is itself supported by another statement.
The IEP defines an extended argument as one with at least one premise that a reasoner attempts to support explicitly.
Van Cleave's Pompeii example has the same shape: one statement supported by a premise then supports the main conclusion.
The IEP's lost-keys example shows the conclusion 'the keys are not in the kitchen' then serving as a premise for 'the keys are in the bedroom'.
The IEP's extended argument has a first step supporting 'the keys are not in the kitchen', which in turn supports the final conclusion 'the keys are in the bedroom'.
